overview: The atlas’s modern Cambodia record begins in 1960 and remains open-ended. It spans sharply different governments, war, genocide and rebuilding; it is not one uninterrupted royal regime. The outline represents a country at coarse intervals, not the territories controlled by each wartime faction. Its first slice even runs across several changes of government before 1994. Earlier Cambodian kingdoms have their own records, while the modern country includes Khmer-majority and minority communities with distinct languages and histories.

periods.title: Sangkum-era kingdom
periods.summary: Sihanouk’s political order governed an independent Cambodia increasingly affected by regional war.

periods.title: Khmer Republic and civil war
periods.summary: The 1970 coup removed Sihanouk; the republic fought communist forces during a widening war.

periods.title: Democratic Kampuchea
periods.summary: Khmer Rouge rule imposed forced transfers and labor amid mass death.

periods.title: People’s Republic of Kampuchea
periods.summary: Vietnamese forces ousted the Khmer Rouge government; the Vietnamese-backed new state faced continuing conflict.

periods.title: State of Cambodia and peace transition
periods.summary: The government adopted the State of Cambodia name in 1989. Peace negotiations and a United Nations mission followed.

periods.title: Constitutional monarchy
periods.summary: A new constitution restored the monarchy in 1993. Governments, public services and political conditions continued changing afterward.

items.text: Cambodia became independent from France on 9 November 1953, before this map record begins. Prince Norodom Sihanouk’s Sangkum political movement dominated the following era. In March 1970, Lon Nol overthrew his administration, leading to the Khmer Republic. Sihanouk then allied from abroad with forces opposing the republic, including Cambodian communists.

After taking Phnom Penh in April 1975, the Khmer Rouge forced residents into the countryside. People endured coercive labor, hunger, disease and executions. The ECCC’s historical account gives an estimated 1.5 to 2 million deaths during April 1975 toJanuary 1979. The loss of state power in 1979 did not immediately end Khmer Rouge armed activity.

The Khmer Rouge period included genocide and crimes against humanity. In 2022, the ECCC’s Supreme Court Chamber upheld Khieu Samphan’s conviction for genocide against the Vietnamese, alongside other crimes, and affirmed his life sentence. That specific legal finding should be distinguished from the broader death toll across Cambodia’s many victim groups.

Court evidence also records couples forced into marriages they had not chosen, often without parents present. The arrangements varied by place and time, but coercion damaged the family support that weddings could otherwise provide. Women and men both suffered. These were abuses imposed by the regime, not a timeless Cambodian marriage custom.

Vietnamese troops defeated the Khmer Rouge government in January 1979, and a Vietnamese-backed People’s Republic of Kampuchea was established. Fighting continued. The government became the State of Cambodia in 1989; the UN records that Vietnam announced its troop withdrawal that September without international verification.

The 1991 Paris agreements opened a negotiated transition. UNTAC organized the 1993 elections and supported human-rights education, refugee return and mine clearance. Its mission account records training about 2,300 Cambodians in clearing mines. The constitution promulgated on 24 September 1993 established a constitutional monarchy, although the settlement did not instantly remove every armed or political conflict.

Tuol Sleng, a former school turned into the S-21 prison, now preserves a deeply troubling archive. Photographs, biographies and prison documents help families and historians trace people who were persecuted. Many supposed confessions were extracted under torture and cannot be treated as truthful admissions. UNESCO registered the archive in 2009.

Work in garments, tourism and construction helped many households increase their incomes. A 2022 World Bank assessment estimated that national poverty fell from 33.8 percent to 17.8 percent over the decade ending in 2019/20. COVID-19 then interrupted livelihoods and pushed some families back into poverty. This dated measure describes a major gain and a setback, not a current household census.

At Srer Chhouk Primary School in Kratie, children once took turns carrying heavy buckets from the well. UNICEF reported in 2025 that improved toilets and handwashing facilities included separate and accessible spaces, soap and mirrors. Pupils could spend less time hauling water; some also enjoyed checking their hair. A useful bathroom can have a small social life of its own.

Ratanakiri’s multilingual schools serve many children from ethnic-minority communities. A UNICEF report published in 2024 described a primary school where an automatic pumping system let children turn on a tap instead of filling and carrying buckets. Remote schools still faced uneven facilities, showing why language access and practical school infrastructure both matter.

Community malaria workers brought testing, treatment and mosquito nets closer to remote households. Mobile workers traveled by boat, motorbike or on foot to reach forest-going populations. In April 2026, WHO reported a decline from 170,387 recorded cases in 1997 to 107 in 2025. It still described remaining challenges and the need for certification, rather than declaring the country malaria-free.

The checked krama cloth can become a scarf, belt, blanket or even a child’s hammock. UNESCO’s 2024 listing describes cotton or silk woven on handlooms, with women predominating in weaving and others helping grow cotton, prepare dyes and maintain looms. Skills pass through families, workshops and producer groups. One rectangle can have a remarkably busy day.

A modern Khmer writing sample is ជាតិ សាសនា ព្រះមហាក្សត្រ, meaning “Nation, Religion, King.” This motto appears in Article 4 of the constitution, including the Senate-hosted Khmer edition checked here. The words are shown in modern type; they are a constitutional witness to Khmer writing, not a claim that every Cambodian shares the same political or religious views.

Parliament approved Hun Manet as prime minister on 22 August 2023. A UN report covering 2023-24 also described restrictions on public expression and the marginalization of opposition groups around the elections. Formal constitutional promises and actual political conditions must therefore be examined separately. These are dated observations about government, not descriptions of the beliefs of all Cambodians.

Recovery remains vulnerable to new shocks. In July 2025, UNICEF reported that fighting along the Cambodia-Thailand border displaced families and interrupted schooling. Schools and pagodas sheltered people, while responders supplied hygiene materials, arranged latrines and supported temporary learning. This is a dated example of civilian needs; a national outline cannot show what each affected family experienced.

ending.text: Cambodia continues as a country, while the regimes within this record have ended or transformed at different times. The 1993 constitutional monarchy followed republics and a peace transition; it must not be projected backward over Khmer Rouge rule. The atlas’s open-ended range signifies continuing coverage, not an assurance of unchanging government or borders.
